concepts.name: Business logic in ViewModels, UI logic in plain state holders

questions.prompt: A Java interface `Game<T>` declares `@NotNull T load(@NotNull T x)`, where `T` may be nullable on the Kotlin side. Your Kotlin interface `ArcadeGame<T1> : Game<T1>` overrides `load`. Which signature does the Kotlin documentation use?

choices.text: `override fun load(x: T1): T1`, since a Kotlin type parameter is never null
`override fun load(x: T1 & Any): T1 & Any`, a definitely non-nullable type
`override fun load(x: T1!!): T1!!`, the not-null assertion applied to a type
`override fun <T1 : Any> load(x: T1): T1`, adding a non-null upper bound

questions.explanation: `T1 & Any` declares a definitely non-nullable version of a type parameter whose upper bound is nullable, which is exactly what Java's `@NotNull T` means. A plain `T1` can still be a nullable type here, `T1!!` is not valid type syntax (`!!` is an expression operator), and declaring a new type parameter `<T1 : Any>` on the function would not override the interface's method. In pure Kotlin you rarely write `& Any`, because inference handles it.

sources.title: Generics: in, out, where
sources.claim: To override a Java method with `@NotNull T` parameters and return, Kotlin declares the type as definitely non-nullable with `T & Any`; a definitely non-nullable type must have a nullable upper bound, and in pure Kotlin inference usually makes it unnecessary.

questions.prompt: A `ReportService` needs a brand-new `ReportBuilder` (an unscoped binding) for every report, and an expensive `PdfEngine` created only on first use and then reused. Which constructor parameter types fit Dagger and Hilt?

choices.text: `ReportBuilder` and `PdfEngine`, both injected directly as is

questions.explanation: `Provider.get()` computes a new value on each call for an unscoped binding, so it suits one builder per report. `Lazy.get()` computes the value on the first call and returns the same result afterwards, so the engine is created only when needed and then reused. Injecting directly creates the value before it is used, and scoping `PdfEngine` as a singleton still creates it eagerly at injection; swapping the two wrappers gets both behaviours backwards.

sources.title: Lazy (Dagger API)
sources.claim: Direct injection computes the value before use, `Provider.get()` computes a new value each time it is called, and `Lazy.get()` computes the value on the first call and returns the same result for every later call on that `Lazy` instance.

questions.prompt: A search screen's ViewModel saves recent searches through a repository, but it also holds the `NavController` and decides from the window size class whether to show a bottom bar or a navigation rail. What would you change, and why?

model_answer.summary: Keep the business logic (saving searches) and the screen's UI state in the ViewModel, and move the UI logic that depends on UI-scoped objects, like the `NavController` and window size, into a plain state holder class the UI creates and remembers.
key_points: Saving recent searches is business logic (a product requirement for app data), so it stays in the ViewModel, which calls the data or domain layer and is retained across Activity recreation
Choosing a bottom bar or a rail, and navigating, is UI logic: it is about how to display state, so it belongs in the UI or a plain class state holder

A plain state holder (like Now in Android's `NiaAppState`) can hold UI-scoped references such as the `NavController` and window size class, because the UI creates it (with `remember` in Compose) and it has the same lifecycle as the UI
A ViewModel is retained through Activity recreation and outlives the UI, so it should not hold UI-scoped objects; a plain holder doesn't survive recreation and can be reused across UIs

questions.explanation: The guide splits state holders by the kind of logic. Business logic and screen UI state go to the ViewModel because it survives configuration changes and reaches the data layer. UI logic that needs UI-scoped objects goes to a plain class with the UI's own lifecycle. Moving everything into the ViewModel is the tempting answer, but it ties a long-lived object to things that are recreated with the UI.

sources.title: State holders and UI state
sources.claim: Business logic implements product requirements for app data and is held by the ViewModel, which is retained through Activity recreation; UI logic is about how to display state (for example navigation or showing a bottom bar) and fits a plain class state holder that references UI-scoped sources, has the UI's lifecycle, is created with `remember`, and doesn't survive Activity recreation.

questions.prompt: What does `T & Any` mean in Kotlin, when do you need to write it, and why do you rarely see it in pure Kotlin code?

model_answer.summary: `T & Any` is a definitely non-nullable version of a type parameter with a nullable bound; you mainly need it to match Java generic APIs annotated `@NotNull`, since in pure Kotlin type inference handles this for you.
key_points: `T & Any` declares the generic type `T` as definitely non-nullable, even though `T` itself may be nullable
It only applies to a type parameter with a nullable upper bound (such as the default `Any?`), with `Any` on the right of `&`
Its main use is interoperability: overriding or implementing a Java generic method whose parameters or return are `@NotNull T`
In code that is only Kotlin you rarely need it, because type inference works out definitely non-nullable types for you

questions.explanation: The feature exists for Java interop: a Java `@NotNull T` has no other exact Kotlin spelling when `T` can be nullable. Writing `<T : Any>` instead changes the type parameter for every use, which is not the same as one non-null use of a nullable `T`.

sources.title: Generics: in, out, where
sources.claim: Kotlin supports declaring a generic type parameter as definitely non-nullable with `T & Any` to make interoperability with generic Java classes easier; it must have a nullable upper bound, and when working only with Kotlin you are unlikely to need it because inference takes care of it.

questions.prompt: `PdfEngine` is an unscoped binding. `ScreenA` and `ScreenB` each inject a `Lazy<PdfEngine>`, and each calls `get()` twice. How many `PdfEngine` instances does Dagger create?

choices.text: One, because every `Lazy` of a type shares a single cached value
Two: each `Lazy` computes once and then remembers its own value
Four, because an unscoped binding is created on every `get()` call
One per component, since `Lazy` behaves like a scope annotation

questions.explanation: Each injected `Lazy` is independent and remembers its value in isolation, so `ScreenA`'s and `ScreenB`'s `Lazy` each create one engine: two in total. Repeated `get()` calls on the same `Lazy` return the same result, so it isn't four. `Lazy` is not a scope: to share one instance across clients you scope the binding, for example with `@Singleton`.

sources.title: Lazy (Dagger API)
sources.claim: All calls to the same `Lazy` instance return the same result, and each injected `Lazy` is independent and remembers its value in isolation of other `Lazy` instances; sharing one instance needs a scope such as `@Singleton`.

questions.prompt: You build a search bar used on three screens. It has its own query text and expanded state and needs no business logic. Which state holder does the state-holder guide recommend for it?

choices.text: A plain state holder class, created and remembered by the UI itself
Its own `ViewModel`, so the query survives configuration changes
The host screen's `ViewModel`, passed down into the search bar
A `@Singleton` holder from Hilt, shared by all three of the screens

questions.explanation: Plain class state holders are recommended for reusable pieces of UI like search bars or chip groups: they hold UI logic and UI element state, follow the UI's lifecycle and can be reused. ViewModels are best for navigation destinations and access to business logic, and passing a screen's ViewModel down couples the component to it, making it harder to reuse, test and preview.

sources.title: State holders and UI state
sources.claim: Plain class state holders are recommended for reusable pieces of UI like search bars or chip groups; ViewModels shouldn't be used there because they are best used for navigation destinations and access to business logic, and ViewModel instances shouldn't be passed down to other composables.
